usage: ㅡ in 쁘 drops, then 어요 attaches → 예뻐요
present modifier: adjective stem + ㄴ (예쁘 → 예쁜)
예쁘 + 게 turns it into the adverb 'prettily'
examples: 이 가방이 정말 예뻐요.
This bag is really pretty.
Plain 요-form to compliment a thing — notice 예쁘 loses its ㅡ before 어요.
예쁜 신발을 사고 싶어요.
I want to buy pretty shoes.
The modifier 예쁜 sits directly in front of the noun it describes (예쁜 + 신발).
오늘 머리 진짜 예쁘다!
Your hair looks so pretty today!
Casual 반말 exclamation 예쁘다 you'd say to a close friend — warm, complimentary.
nuance: 예쁘다 means pretty, lovely, or cute-attractive, and is the everyday compliment Koreans pay to things, people, scenery, even babies and handwriting. Conjugation rests on the 으-irregular (흔히 'ㅡ 탈락'): the bare ㅡ in 쁘 simply drops before an ending that starts with a vowel, so 예쁘 + 어요 → 예뻐요, never 예쁘어요. The present modifier is 예쁜 (stem + ㄴ). Its closest near-synonym is 아름답다, and the dividing line is register and scale: 예쁘다 is warm, casual, and personal ('cute and pretty'), while 아름답다 is grander, more literary and emotional ('beautiful, sublime') — a flower or a girl's outfit is 예뻐요, but a sunset or a symphony is 아름다워요. 귀엽다 leans 'adorable/charming', not just visually pretty. It habitually pairs with 정말/너무/참 (정말 예뻐요) and with 옷·얼굴·꽃·글씨. The English-speaker pitfall: do not write 예쁘어요 (forgetting the ㅡ drops), and remember the subject takes 이/가 (꽃이 예뻐요), because 예쁘다 is a descriptive adjective, not an action you do to an object.

mistakes: Saying 예쁘어요 instead of 예뻐요 — 예쁘다 is 으-irregular, so the ㅡ in 쁘 drops before 어요 (예쁘 → 예뻐요).
Marking the thing with 을/를 (가방을 예뻐요) — 예쁘다 is an adjective describing a state, so its subject takes 이/가: 가방이 예뻐요.
Using 예쁘다 for grand, sublime beauty (석양이 예뻐요 for a breathtaking sunset) — for that elevated sense 아름답다 (석양이 아름다워요) fits better; 예쁘다 stays casual and personal.

usage: 있다-type takes 는 as its present modifier, not 은
examples: 그 배우가 정말 멋있어요.
That actor is really cool.
Standard 요-form admiring a person — 멋있 + 어요, no vowel change.
멋있는 옷을 입고 싶어요.
I want to wear stylish clothes.
The modifier of an 있다-type word is 멋있는 (with 는), placed before 옷.
와, 그 차 진짜 멋있다.
Wow, that car is so cool.
Casual 반말 멋있다 of admiration — the everyday way to say 'that's awesome/cool'.
nuance: 멋있다 means cool, stylish, or impressively attractive — it admires a quality of taste, presence, or charisma, not mere prettiness. Built on 멋 ('style, flair, dash') + 있다 ('to have'), it literally says 'has flair', which is exactly why it conjugates as an 있다-type word: its present modifier is 멋있는 (like 재미있는, 맛있는), NOT 멋있은. Its near-identical twin is 멋지다, and the line is subtle: 멋있다 and 멋지다 are largely interchangeable ('cool/awesome'), but 멋지다 sounds a touch more exclamatory and is slightly more common in spontaneous praise (멋지다!), while 멋있다 can describe a steady, ongoing coolness. Contrast both with 예쁘다 (visually pretty) and 잘생기다 (good-looking of facial features) — a man with great style is 멋있어요 even if you wouldn't call him 예뻐요. It collocates with 사람·차·옷·모습·자세 and with intensifiers 정말/진짜/너무. The English-speaker pitfall: write 멋있는 not 멋있은 for the modifier, and never 멋있다 with 을/를 — the admired thing takes 이/가 (그 사람이 멋있어요).

usage: stem 길 + 어요 (the ㄹ stays before a vowel)
ㄹ-irregular: final ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ (길 → 긴)
길 + 게 → adverb 'lengthily/in a long way'
examples: 이 길이 너무 길어요.
This road is too long.
요-form 길어요; the ㄹ is kept because 어 is a vowel ending.
긴 치마를 입었어요.
I wore a long skirt.
The modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ, giving 긴 (not 길은) before 치마.
기다리는 시간이 길어서 지쳤어요.
The waiting time was long, so I got tired.
길어서 (요-form + 서) gives the reason 'because it was long'.
nuance: 길다 means long in physical length (긴 머리, 긴 다리) and equally in duration of time (긴 하루 = a long day, 시간이 길다 = the time is long). Its conjugation is the textbook ㄹ-irregular: the stem ㄹ survives before vowel endings (길어요) but vanishes before the modifier ㄴ, so 'long hair' is 긴 머리, never 길은 머리 — the same drop you see in 멀다→먼, 달다→단. Its plain opposite is 짧다 (short). The subtle trap is the time sense: when an event happens 'long ago / early', that is 오래다/오래되다 or the adverb 오래, NOT 길다 — 길다 measures a span's extent, not a point's distance in the past (so 'I've waited long' = 오래 기다렸어요, but 'the wait is long' = 기다림이 길어요). It collocates with 머리·다리·치마·줄·시간·연설. English-speaker pitfalls: don't write 길은 for the modifier (it must be 긴), and don't reach for 길다 to mean 'a long time ago' — that role belongs to 오래.

usage: last stem vowel is ㅏ, so 아요 attaches → 짧아요
짧 + 게 → adverb 'short(ly)' with an action verb
examples: 이 바지가 좀 짧아요.
These pants are a bit short.
요-form 짧아요; vowel harmony picks 아요 because the stem vowel is ㅏ.
짧은 글을 한 편 썼어요.
I wrote one short piece of writing.
Regular modifier 짧은 (stem + 은) before 글, since the stem ends in a consonant cluster.
방학이 짧아서 아쉬워요.
The vacation is short, so it's a shame.
짧아서 gives the reason 'because it's short'; pairs naturally with 아쉽다.
nuance: 짧다 means short — in length (짧은 머리, 짧은 치마), in duration (짧은 시간), and figuratively in 'lacking' (실력이 짧다 = one's skill is shallow/limited). It is the straightforward opposite of 길다. Conjugation is regular: the final stem vowel ㅏ triggers 아요 (짧아요) by vowel harmony, and the modifier is 짧은 (stem + 은); the double-consonant batchim ㄼ is fully written but only ㄹ is pronounced, so 짧다 sounds like '짤따'. Watch the synonym boundary with 낮다 ('low in height') and 작다 ('small in size'): a short skirt's hem is 짧다 (short in length), but a low ceiling is 낮다 and a small bag is 작다 — English lumps several of these under 'short/small', Korean does not. It collocates with 머리·치마·바지·시간·거리·글. English-speaker pitfalls: don't write 짧어요 (vowel harmony demands 아요, not 어요), and don't use 짧다 for a person being 'short in height' — that is 키가 작다 (literally 'small in stature'), never 키가 짧다.

usage: 르-irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ before 아요 (빠르 → 빨ㄹ + 아요)
modifier is regular: stem + ㄴ (빠르 → 빠른)
빠르 + 게 → adverb 'quickly', common with motion verbs
examples: 이 기차가 정말 빨라요.
This train is really fast.
르-irregular in action: 빠르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ → 빨라요, never 빠르어요.
빠른 답장을 받아서 기뻤어요.
I was glad to get a quick reply.
The modifier 빠른 is regular (빠르 + ㄴ) and sits before 답장.
조금만 더 빨리 와 주세요.
Please come just a little faster.
The set adverb 빨리 ('quickly') is the form you'll hear most in daily speech.
nuance: 빠르다 means fast or quick — high in speed, whether a train, the internet, a reply, or a person's pace. Its conjugation is the classic 르-irregular: before an 아/어 ending the 르 splits into ㄹㄹ and the previous syllable gains a ㄹ batchim, so 빠르 + 아요 → 빨라요 (never 빠르어요 or 빠라요); the modifier 빠른, however, is perfectly regular. The crucial synonym contrast is 이르다 ('early in time'): 빠르다 is about SPEED (how fast something moves), while 이르다 is about TIMING (how early on the clock/calendar) — '버스가 빨라요' means the bus is fast, but '아직 일러요' means 'it's still early'. English 'fast' and 'early' both hide here, so don't say 빨라요 to mean 'it's early'. The everyday adverb is the irregular set form 빨리 (빨리 오세요), distinct from the regular 빠르게. It collocates with 기차·차·인터넷·발·답장 and with 정말/너무. English-speaker pitfall: producing 빠라요 (forgetting to double the ㄹ) or 빠르어요 (ignoring the irregular), and confusing speed-빠르다 with time-이르다.

Using 빠르다 to mean 'early' (지금 가기엔 빨라요 for 'it's too early to go') — that is 이르다: 가기엔 일러요. 빠르다 is speed, 이르다 is timing.
Saying 빠르게 오세요 where natives prefer the set adverb — the idiomatic 'come quickly' is 빨리 오세요 (빨리 is the irregular adverb of 빠르다).

usage: last stem vowel ㅗ → 아요 by vowel harmony (높 → 높아요)
높 + 게 → adverb 'high(ly)' with an action verb
examples: 저 산이 아주 높아요.
That mountain is very high.
요-form 높아요; the stem vowel ㅗ selects 아요, and the ㅍ links to give a '노파요' sound.
높은 빌딩을 처음 봤어요.
I saw a tall building for the first time.
The regular modifier 높은 (stem + 은) precedes 빌딩.
가격이 너무 높아서 안 샀어요.
The price was too high, so I didn't buy it.
높아서 marks the reason; note 가격이 높다 is the natural pairing for 'price is high'.
nuance: 높다 means high or tall and also 'high in level' for abstractions — mountains and buildings (산이 높다, 빌딩이 높다), but also 가격이 높다 (price is high), 온도가 높다 (temperature is high), 소리가 높다 (pitch is high), and 가능성이 높다 (the likelihood is high). Conjugation is regular: vowel ㅗ takes 아요 (높아요), modifier is 높은. The key synonym boundary is with 크다 ('big/large') for people: a person's height is described with 키가 크다 (literally 'stature is big'), NOT 키가 높다 — 높다 is for objects rising from a base (a tower, a shelf), while a human's tallness is 키가 크다. Its opposites split too: 높다 ↔ 낮다 (low), but 크다 ↔ 작다 (small). It collocates with 산·건물·가격·온도·소리·확률·수준. English-speaker pitfall: 'a tall person' becomes 높은 사람 by direct translation, which sounds like 'a high-ranking/lofty person', not 'a tall one' — say 키가 큰 사람; reserve 높다 for things that stand high off the ground.

usage: stem 멀 + 어요 (the ㄹ stays before a vowel)
ㄹ-irregular: final ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ (멀 → 먼)
멀 → the set adverb 멀리 'far (away)', used with motion verbs
examples: 집이 회사에서 멀어요.
My home is far from work.
요-form 멀어요; the reference point takes 에서 ('from'), as in 회사에서 멀다.
먼 나라로 여행을 가요.
I'm traveling to a faraway country.
The modifier drops ㄹ before ㄴ → 먼 (not 멀은) before 나라.
역이 멀어서 버스를 타요.
The station is far, so I take the bus.
멀어서 gives the reason 'because it's far'.
nuance: 멀다 means far in distance (집이 멀다, 먼 길) and figuratively 'distant' in relationship or likelihood (사이가 멀어지다 = to grow apart; 거리가 멀다). It is the opposite of 가깝다 (near). Conjugation is ㄹ-irregular: the ㄹ stays before vowel endings (멀어요) but drops before the modifier ㄴ, so 'a far place' is 먼 곳, never 멀은 곳 — the same pattern as 길다→긴, 달다→단. The natural way to say the distance is FROM somewhere is with 에서: 여기에서 멀어요 ('it's far from here'). Note the set adverb is the irregular 멀리 ('far away', 멀리 가다), not 멀게. A subtle synonym point: for 'a remote/secluded place' Korean often prefers 외지다 or 외딴, while 멀다 is plain physical distance. It collocates with 집·학교·역·길·나라·거리·미래. English-speaker pitfalls: writing 멀은 for the modifier instead of 먼, and marking the reference with the wrong particle — say 회사에서 멀어요 (from work), not 회사에 멀어요.

Writing 멀은 for the modifier instead of 먼, and marking the reference with the wrong particle — say 회사에서 멀어요 (from work), not 회사에 멀어요.

mistakes: Saying 멀은 곳 instead of 먼 곳 — 멀다 is ㄹ-irregular, so the ㄹ drops before the modifier ㄴ: 멀 → 먼.
Marking the reference point with 에 (회사에 멀어요) — 'far FROM X' uses 에서: 회사에서 멀어요.
Using 멀게 for 'far away' as an adverb — the idiomatic adverb is the irregular 멀리: 멀리 가다 (멀게 is grammatical but not what natives say for distance).

usage: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가까워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가깝 → 가까운)
the set adverb 가까이 'near/close', used with motion verbs
examples: 지하철역이 가까워요.
The subway station is close.
ㅂ-irregular in action: 가깝 + 어요 → ㅂ turns to 우 → 가까워요, not 가깝아요.
가까운 친구를 오랜만에 만났어요.
I met a close friend after a long time.
The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가까운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 친구; note 가까운 친구 = a close (intimate) friend.
회사가 가까워서 걸어 다녀요.
Work is close, so I commute on foot.
가까워서 gives the reason 'because it's close'.
nuance: 가깝다 means close or near in distance (집이 가깝다), and just as commonly 'close' in human relationships (가까운 사이 = an intimate relationship) and 'nearly equal' (백 명에 가깝다 = close to 100). It is the opposite of 멀다 (far). Its conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: the final ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel ending, so 가깝 + 어요 → 가까워요 and the modifier is 가까운 (never 가깝아요 or 가깝은) — the same shift as 무겁다→무거워, 어렵다→어려워. A useful synonym boundary: 가깝다 is the adjective ('is near'), while the place noun 근처 means 'the vicinity/nearby area' (역 근처에 = near the station) and the adverb 가까이 means 'closely/up near' (가까이 오세요) — they aren't interchangeable parts of speech. It collocates with 집·역·거리·사이·친구 and with the distance reference in 에서 (여기에서 가까워요). English-speaker pitfalls: writing 가깝아요 (ignoring the ㅂ-irregular), and confusing the adjective 가깝다 with the noun 근처 — 'there's a store nearby' is best as 근처에 가게가 있어요, not 가깝다 alone.

usage: 하다-verb: 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 → 깨끗해요
깨끗하 + 게 → adverb 'cleanly/spotlessly' with an action verb
examples: 이 화장실이 깨끗해요.
This bathroom is clean.
하다-pattern: 깨끗하 + 여요 contracts to 깨끗해요 (the standard 해요-form).
깨끗한 물을 마셔요.
I drink clean water.
The 하다-modifier 깨끗한 (하 + ㄴ) precedes 물.
방을 깨끗이 치웠어요.
I tidied the room cleanly.
The set adverb 깨끗이 (note spelling: -이, sounds '깨끄시') is the idiomatic 'cleanly/thoroughly'.
nuance: 깨끗하다 means clean — free of dirt (깨끗한 방), but also 'pure/clear' for water and air (깨끗한 물·공기), 'fair/honest' for conduct (깨끗한 정치 = clean politics), and 'fully/completely' as the adverb 깨끗이 (깨끗이 잊다 = to forget completely). Being a 하다-adjective, it conjugates with the 해요-pattern: the 하 fuses with 여 to give 깨끗해요, and the modifier is 깨끗한 — there is no irregular drop here, just the regular 하다 contraction. Watch the synonym line with 맑다: 맑다 is 'clear/limpid' for water, sky, eyes, or sound (하늘이 맑다 = the sky is clear; 물이 맑다 = the water is transparent), whereas 깨끗하다 is 'free of dirt/impurity' (물이 깨끗하다 = the water is clean/sanitary). So a mountain stream can be both 맑다 (see-through) and 깨끗하다 (unpolluted), but a tidy desk is only 깨끗하다, never 맑다. It collocates with 방·옷·물·공기·손·거리. English-speaker pitfall: writing 깨끗하요 (forgetting the 하 → 해 contraction) and spelling the adverb 깨끗히 instead of the correct 깨끗이.

usage: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 무거워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (무겁 → 무거운)
무겁 + 게 → adverb 'heavily', also for atmosphere/mood
examples: 이 가방이 너무 무거워요.
This bag is too heavy.
ㅂ-irregular: 무겁 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 무거워요, never 무겁어요.
무거운 상자를 혼자 옮겼어요.
I moved a heavy box by myself.
The ㅂ-irregular modifier 무거운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 상자.
눈꺼풀이 무거워서 졸려요.
My eyelids are heavy, so I'm sleepy.
무거워서 gives the reason; 눈꺼풀이 무겁다 is the idiomatic 'eyelids feel heavy (sleepy)'.
nuance: 무겁다 means heavy in weight (무거운 가방, 짐이 무겁다), and metaphorically 'weighty/grave' for moods, responsibilities, and the body when tired — 분위기가 무겁다 (the atmosphere is heavy/tense), 책임이 무겁다 (the responsibility is heavy), 몸이 무겁다 (one's body feels sluggish), 입이 무겁다 (literally 'heavy-mouthed' = tight-lipped, can keep a secret). It is the opposite of 가볍다 (light). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, giving 무거워요 and the modifier 무거운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 춥다→추워. Be careful with 무겁다 vs 어렵다: both can render English 'heavy' figuratively, but 무겁다 is 'weighty/somber', whereas 어렵다 is 'difficult' — a heavy (hard) exam is 어려운 시험, not 무거운 시험. It collocates with 가방·짐·몸·분위기·책임·마음. English-speaker pitfall: producing 무겁어요 instead of 무거워요, and over-extending 무겁다 to mean 'difficult' where 어렵다 is needed.

usage: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 가벼워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (가볍 → 가벼운)
examples: 이 노트북이 정말 가벼워요.
This laptop is really light.
ㅂ-irregular: 가볍 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.
가벼운 가방을 하나 샀어요.
I bought one light bag.
The ㅂ-irregular modifier 가벼운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 가방.
오늘은 마음이 한결 가벼워요.
Today my heart feels much lighter.
마음이 가볍다 = to feel relieved/unburdened — a common figurative use.
nuance: 가볍다 means light in weight (가벼운 가방), and figuratively 'light' in many senses: 마음이 가볍다 (heart is light/relieved), 가벼운 감기 (a mild cold), 가벼운 농담 (a light joke), 가볍게 운동하다 (to exercise lightly), and even negatively 입이 가볍다 ('light-mouthed' = can't keep a secret, the exact opposite of 입이 무겁다). It is the opposite of 무겁다 (heavy). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel ending, so 가벼워요 and the modifier 가벼운 — the same pattern as 무겁다→무거워, 춥다→추워. A synonym note: 가볍다 covers 'light/mild', but 'easy' (simple to do) is 쉽다, so 'an easy question' is 쉬운 문제, not 가벼운 문제 — though 가벼운 문제 can mean a 'minor/trivial' issue. Be careful too that 'light' as in brightness/color is 밝다 (밝은 색 = a light/bright color), not 가볍다. It collocates with 가방·노트북·옷·마음·발걸음·농담·감기. usage: ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, then 어요 → 새로워요
ㅂ-irregular modifier: ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ (새롭 → 새로운)
examples: 이 식당이 새로워요.
This restaurant is new.
ㅂ-irregular: 새롭 + 어요 → ㅂ to 우 → 새로워요, not 새롭어요.
새로운 휴대폰을 샀어요.
I bought a new phone.
The ㅂ-irregular modifier 새로운 (ㅂ → 우 + ㄴ) precedes 휴대폰 — the everyday way to say 'a new ~'.
다시 보니 그 풍경이 새로워요.
Seeing it again, that scenery feels fresh.
Here 새롭다 means 'feels new/striking again', the emotional 'fresh' sense, not 'newly made'.
nuance: 새롭다 means new in the sense of 'fresh, novel, renewed' — a new method, a fresh feeling, a renewed resolve (새로운 방법, 마음이 새롭다, 각오가 새롭다). Crucially it differs from the determiner 새 ('brand-new', placed directly before a noun): 새 (no conjugation) labels a physically new object — 새 차 (a brand-new car), 새 옷 (new clothes) — while 새롭다 is a full adjective expressing that something is novel or feels fresh, so '새 차' is a car just bought, but '느낌이 새로워요' means 'the feeling is fresh/novel'. Both translate as 'new', but you cannot say 새로운 차 to mean a factory-fresh car the way 새 차 does (새로운 차 leans 'a different/novel kind of car'). Conjugation is the ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 우, giving 새로워요 and the modifier 새로운 — the same shift as 가깝다→가까워, 무겁다→무거워. It collocates with 방법·기술·세상·마음·각오·디자인. English-speaker pitfall: writing 새롭어요 instead of 새로워요, and reaching for 새롭다 when you mean a plain brand-new object — for that, the short determiner 새 (새 신발, 새 집) is what natives use.
